samples.question: The picture shows three separate blocks of dot tallies on a plain background: one near the top-left corner, one near the top-right corner and one near the bottom centre of the page. Nothing joins the three blocks and the space between them is empty. Each block holds exactly four tallies arranged as two rows of two, so every block has an upper-left, an upper-right, a lower-left and a lower-right position, and the same four position names are used in all three blocks. A tally is a single horizontal row of small solid squares; every square in the picture has the same size and the squares of a tally are evenly spaced, so the only thing that distinguishes one tally from another is how many squares it holds. Every tally holds between two and eight squares. Exactly one of the four positions holds the same number of squares in all three blocks. Each of the other three positions holds the same number of squares in exactly two of the three blocks and a clearly different number in the remaining one, and the three wrong positions are shared out over the three different pairs of blocks, so whichever two blocks you compare you will find a second position that also seems to agree. All three blocks must therefore be read: no two of them can single out the answer, and no block on its own carries any information about it. The answer is not revealed by ink colour, by exactly where the blocks sit, by which block holds the odd tally of a position, or by amount of ink: inside any single block the answer position is never the one with the most squares nor the one with the fewest, and its total over the three blocks is equally often the largest, the second, the third and the smallest of the four positions. Which block position holds the same number of squares in all three blocks? Answer with one of: upper-left, upper-right, lower-left, lower-right.
